memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Then he made two cherubim out of hammered gold at the ends of the cover. He made one cherub on one end and the second cherub on the other; at the two ends he made them of one piece with the cover. The cherubim had their wings spread upwards, overshadowing the cover with them. The cherubim faced each other, looking towards the cover." - Exod 37:7-9 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Two angelic figures, wings spread, faces turned downward toward the blood-sprinkled cover.

Remember where cherubim last appeared: at the entrance to Eden, guarding the way back to the tree of life after humanity was shut out (Gen 3:24). They stood as a barrier. Here, they stand and gaze at the place where atonement is made.

Even angels are studying this. Peter writes that the prophets searched intently into the salvation to come, and that even angels long to look into these things (1 Pet 1:10-12). The mercy of God toward sinners is the most fascinating subject in the universe, and heaven itself leans in to watch.

Notice they are hammered from one piece with the cover. They are not attached; they belong to it. Mercy and the worship of heaven are inseparable.

And notice where they are not looking — not at each other, not outward at the people, but down at the place of atonement.

That is a good picture of where our attention belongs. Not on ourselves, not on comparing with others, but on what God has done in Christ.

If angels find this endlessly interesting, why do we grow bored with the gospel so quickly?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Has the gospel become ordinary to you?
2. Where is your attention most naturally drawn?
3. What would it look like to wonder at God's mercy again this week?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, forgive me for growing casual about the greatest thing in the universe. Restore my wonder at Your mercy. Amen.
